short: The Persian title for a king.
note: A Persian royal title, historically used by the rulers of Iran.

short: Lance-armed cavalrymen.
note: Uhlans were light cavalry armed with lances, originally associated with Poland and later with other European armies.

short: One hundredth of a ruble.
note: A Russian monetary unit equal to one hundredth of a ruble; also a coin representing that amount.

short: An older English name for Latvian.
note: Lettish means Latvian: the language of Latvia or something belonging to its people.

short: A member of the Prussian landed nobility.
note: A Junker was a German nobleman, especially a member of the Prussian landowning aristocracy associated with military and political power.

short: A nickname or familiar epithet.
note: An alternative name given to someone, often an affectionate or descriptive nickname. The word comes from French.

short: A Russian country house.
note: A house in the Russian countryside used especially as a seasonal or holiday residence.

short: Members of the old Russian nobility.
note: Boyars were members of the high nobility in Russia and certain other eastern European states.

short: A knight entitled to lead under his own banner.
note: A banneret was a knight of higher military rank entitled to carry a square banner and lead a body of men under it.

short: A knight wandering in search of adventures.
note: In medieval romance, a knight-errant travels in search of adventures, combat, and opportunities to uphold chivalric ideals.

short: A royal title derived from Caesar.
note: The title of an emperor or supreme ruler in Russia and some other Slavic countries. Its linguistic ancestry is the Roman name Caesar.

short: An extensive treeless grassland.
note: A broad, generally dry grassland, particularly characteristic of southeastern Europe and central Asia.

short: A first cousin.
note: An older term for a first cousin: the child of one’s aunt or uncle. German here means closely related.

short: Heated urns for tea water.
note: A samovar is a metal urn used especially in Russia to heat water for tea, traditionally with burning fuel in a central tube.

short: A revered Russian icon of Mary and the infant Christ.
note: The Tikhvin icon depicts the Mother of God holding Christ. Orthodox tradition associates its appearance near Tikhvin with 1383; its feast is June 26.

sources.label: Orthodox Church in America · Tikhvin icon

short: The archangel who leads the heavenly army.
note: Michael is the biblical archangel depicted as a warrior. Revelation 12 describes him and his angels fighting the dragon, identified there as Satan.

short: The monstrous hound guarding the underworld.
note: In Greek and Roman mythology, Cerberus guards the realm of the dead. In Aeneid 6, the Sibyl subdues him with a drugged cake of honey and grain so that she and Aeneas can pass.

short: A death-defying sorcerer of Russian folktales.
note: Koshchei, also transliterated Koschei or Kashchei, is a supernatural antagonist in Russian folklore. “The Death of Koshchei the Deathless” appears in Andrew Lang’s The Red Fairy Book (1890).

sources.label: Andrew Lang · The Red Fairy Book

short: The formidable witch of Russian folktales.
note: Baba Yaga is a witchlike figure in Russian folklore, often associated with a hut on chicken legs and travel in a mortar propelled by a pestle. Depending on the tale, she may threaten or assist a visitor.

sources.label: Andrew Lang · The Red Fairy Book

short: A Baltic trading city and Latvia’s capital.
note: Riga, on the Daugava near the Baltic Sea, became an important Hanseatic trading city during the Middle Ages. It is the capital of Latvia.

short: Reims, the French coronation city.
note: Rheims is an older English spelling of Reims. Its cathedral was the traditional setting for the anointing and coronation of French kings.

sources.label: UNESCO · Reims cathedral and royal sites

short: Charlemagne’s principal royal residence.
note: Aachen is a city in western Germany associated with Charlemagne’s palace and chapel. His chapel became the core of Aachen Cathedral, and he was buried there in 814.

short: The historical German name of Jelgava, Latvia.
note: Mitau is the German name of Jelgava, a Latvian city on the Lielupe. It served as the capital of the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia.

short: The historical German name of Liepāja, Latvia.
note: Libau is the German name of Liepāja, a Baltic seaport in western Latvia, historically part of Courland.

short: Russian for the hazel grouse.
note: Russian ryabchik, рябчик, names the hazel grouse, a small, mottled woodland game bird of Europe and northern Asia.

short: Possibly Russian kinzhal, “dagger.”
note: Possibly Russian kinzhal, meaning a dagger. Kindjal is a related English spelling for the broad, double-edged daggers associated with the Caucasus.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum of Art · Caucasian kindjal

short: An ancient image of truth hidden from human knowledge.
note: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 9.72, attributes to Democritus the saying that truth lies in a well. It expresses how difficult truth is to reach.

short: Possibly Russian speshite: “Hurry!”
note: Possibly a phonetic spelling of Russian speshite, спешите, the plural or polite command “Hurry!” from speshit’, to hurry or hasten.

short: Possibly Russian zaderzhite yego: “Stop him!”
note: Possibly Russian zaderzhite yego, задержите его: “Stop him!” or “Detain him!” Zaderzhat’ means to hold someone back or prevent departure.

short: A German noble title equivalent to count.
note: Graf is a German title of nobility equivalent to count or to the British rank of earl.

short: Cervantes’s idealistic knight-errant.
note: The central figure of Miguel de Cervantes’s Don Quixote, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615. Immersed in chivalric romances, he travels with Sancho Panza seeking knightly adventures.

short: Possibly the flying horse of The Arabian Nights.
note: Possibly the magical wooden mount in “The Enchanted Horse,” a tale from The Arabian Nights. Presented to the Persian king, the horse carries its rider through the air by means of a mechanical control.

sources.label: Andrew Lang · The Arabian Nights Entertainments

short: Possibly the heraldic raven of the Hunyadi family.
note: Possibly the raven emblem of Hungary’s Hunyadi dynasty, associated especially with King Matthias Corvinus. The family’s arms show a raven holding a ring; Corvinus derives from Latin corvus, raven.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum of Art · A Deadly Art

short: The White Eagle, Poland’s national emblem.
note: Poland’s heraldic emblem is a white eagle, traditionally crowned, displayed against a red field. The design developed from medieval Piast heraldry and became the arms of the kingdom.

sources.label: Jan Szczepkowski Museum · The Piast Eagle

short: A kingdom whose ruler is chosen by election.
note: An elective monarchy selects its sovereign through a vote by a designated body. In the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, royal elections were a central privilege of the nobility.

sources.label: Felicia Roșu · Elective Monarchy in Transylvania and Poland-Lithuania

short: The historical German name of Klaipėda, Lithuania.
note: Memel is the German name of Klaipėda, a Baltic port in Lithuania. The town developed around the medieval castle of Memelburg, first mentioned in 1252.

sources.label: Association of Castles and Museums around the Baltic Sea · Klaipėda Castle

short: An ancient fortified settlement near Pskov.
note: Izborsk is a historic settlement in northwestern Russia near Pskov. Its stone fortress on Zheravya Hill was begun in 1330 as part of the region’s frontier defenses.

short: The peoples of the Baltic language family.
note: Balts is a collective name for peoples speaking Baltic languages, including Lithuanians, Latvians, and the historically distinct Old Prussians.

short: Frontier military communities of eastern Europe.
note: Cossacks formed self-governing military communities on the eastern European frontier, notably in Ukraine and southern Russia. Their traditions were strongly associated with horsemanship and armed service.

short: The Dnipro, a major river flowing to the Black Sea.
note: The Dnieper, called Dnipro in Ukrainian, rises in Russia and flows through Belarus and Ukraine to the Black Sea. It has long been a major route of settlement, commerce, and communication.

sources.label: Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine · Dnipro River

short: The luminous magical bird of Russian folktales.
note: The firebird is a marvelous bird of Russian folklore whose feathers shine like flame. A shining feather often sets a hero on a difficult quest.

sources.label: Arthur Ransome · Old Peter’s Russian Tales

short: The elected imperial ruler of the Holy Roman Empire.
note: The Holy Roman Emperor headed a collection of central European territories, predominantly German-speaking. The imperial office was elective, though the Habsburgs held it almost continuously from the fifteenth century until 1806.

sources.label: Schönbrunn Group · The Habsburgs and the Empire
